evidence.excerpt: Manual EMC design review is time-consuming and relies on reviewer expertise that varies across organisations. This paper describes a rule-based layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and a netlist, extracts geometric features related to emission risk, and outputs a numerical score and flagged violation list. Seventeen rules were derived from simulation studies and published guidelines, covering trace-to-plane spacing, clock trace routing distance from board edge, decoupling capacitor placement relative to device power pins, and via stub length. The tool was implemented in Python using open-source Gerber parsing libraries. Validation was performed by scoring 23 PCB designs of known emission performance; boards that failed CISPR 22 Class B measurements scored below the threshold in 19 out of 23 cases (83% sensitivity). False-positive rate was 22%. Run time for a 20-layer board with 4000 components averaged 38 seconds. The tool is intended as an early design gate rather than a replacement for simulation or pre-compliance measurement.

This paper describes an integrated pre-compliance workflow for mixed-signal PCB development that combines three techniques used sequentially across the design cycle. In the early layout phase, an automated rule-checking tool flags geometric violations associated with known emission risks. At the prototype stage, near-field scanning at 3 mm standoff generates spatial emission maps that identify dominant radiating structures. Finally, FDTD simulation using geometry extracted from the identified hotspots provides frequency-resolved quantification and supports what-if analysis of corrective measures. The workflow was applied to four prototype boards developed in collaboration with two regional electronics companies. Across all four boards, the integrated workflow identified the dominant emission source correctly in each case; corrective measures applied on the basis of simulation results reduced the peak radiated emission at the pre-compliance test receiver by between 5.2 dB and 11.7 dB before formal OATS measurement. Time-to-compliance for the four designs averaged 2.1 fewer test-and-rework cycles compared to a historical baseline of designs developed without structured pre-compliance analysis. The workflow documentation and rule-checker code are deposited in an open repository.

Power delivery network (PDN) impedance management in mixed-signal boards is examined through a combined measurement and simulation campaign. A test vehicle carrying an FPGA and two 12-bit ADC devices was designed with three decoupling capacitor placement strategies: bulk capacitors only, distributed 100 nF ceramic capacitors at 5 mm spacing, and a co-planar interdigitated capacitance structure formed by alternating power and ground copper pours. PDN impedance was measured from 100 kHz to 1 GHz using a one-port shunt method with a vector network analyser. Simultaneously, conducted noise on the 3.3 V rail was recorded with a 1 GHz oscilloscope probe during switching activity driven by a test pattern generator. The distributed ceramic strategy reduced peak PDN impedance from 840 mΩ to 210 mΩ at 480 MHz. Radiated emissions pre-compliance scans at 3 m confirmed a corresponding 4.8 dB reduction in broadband noise floor between 400 and 600 MHz. A compact circuit model of the PDN, fitted to measurement data, reproduces impedance to within 8% across the full bandwidth.

This paper investigates whether automated near-field scan data acquired at 3 mm standoff can reliably predict far-field radiated emission rankings before a product undergoes formal OATS testing. Seven commercial-grade consumer electronics boards were scanned on a 150 mm × 150 mm grid with 2 mm step resolution at frequencies from 30 MHz to 1 GHz. Far-field transformation was applied using a planar near-to-far-field algorithm. Results were compared against 3 m OATS measurements performed at an accredited external laboratory. Rank-ordering agreement between pre-compliance near-field predictions and OATS results was 85% at the frequency of maximum emission for each board. Absolute amplitude agreement was within ±4.5 dB in 74% of cases, degrading to ±9 dB at frequencies above 700 MHz where enclosure resonances are significant. The findings suggest the methodology is reliable for early design triage but not as a substitute for final certification. Practical recommendations for scan grid density and probe calibration are provided.

The project developed and validated a structured pre-compliance methodology for predicting radiated and conducted electromagnetic emissions from mixed-signal PCBs before formal certification testing. Work packages covered automated layout rule checking, near-field scan data processing and far-field transformation, and parametric FDTD simulation libraries for common PCB geometries. The methodology was validated on test vehicles designed at the faculty and on prototype boards provided by two partner companies from the Vojvodina electronics manufacturing sector. The project trained two doctoral students and produced seven peer-reviewed publications. An open-source rule-checker tool was released under a permissive licence. The project supported calibration and upgrade of the faculty's near-field scanning bench, including a new motorised Z-axis stage.

Automotive DC–DC converters operating from a 48 V bus generate conducted emissions in the CISPR 25 frequency range (150 kHz–108 MHz) that must be suppressed before reaching the vehicle harness. This paper analyses five commercial common-mode choke families with inductances between 10 µH and 220 µH, characterising their impedance using two-port measurements and fitting a frequency-dependent equivalent circuit that captures core saturation effects at the DC bias levels typical of a 5 A converter. The fitted models were embedded in a SPICE simulation of a full input filter topology and validated against conducted emission measurements using a LISN. Key findings: chokes with ferrite cores exhibited a self-resonance artefact near 3 MHz that produced an emission peak rather than suppression; nanocrystalline core variants maintained greater than 40 dB insertion loss between 1 MHz and 30 MHz under full bias. A selection procedure based on impedance-at-bias rather than inductance-at-zero-bias is proposed and benchmarked against five converter test cases.

Moat-type splits in ground planes, often introduced to isolate analogue and digital regions, are known to increase radiated emissions when high-frequency signals cross them. This study quantifies the effect using method-of-moments modelling of a canonical two-layer board geometry with a 50 Ω microstrip carrying a 200 MHz square-wave clock. Moat widths of 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm, and 2.0 mm were evaluated with and without a 100 nF bridging capacitor placed at the crossing point. The MoM solver was validated by a controlled experiment in a GTEM cell. Without bridging, a 1 mm moat increased the peak radiated electric field at CISPR class B limits by 7.4 dB at the third harmonic (600 MHz). A single bridging capacitor reduced the excess to 1.8 dB. These results are mapped onto a simple analytical expression involving crossing current, moat length, and frequency, allowing designers to estimate the penalty before committing to layout. Limitations of the analytical approximation above 800 MHz are discussed.

Dijana Radulović received her Dipl.-Ing. and M.Sc. degrees in Electrical Engineering from the Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, in 2004 and 2008 respectively, and her Ph.D. from the same institution in 2013. She was appointed Assistant Professor in 2014 and promoted to Associate Professor in 2019 within the Department of Power, Electronics and Telecommunications. Her research group focuses on computational electromagnetic modelling of printed circuit board geometries, signal integrity degradation mechanisms in high-speed mixed-signal designs, and pre-compliance methodologies for reducing radiated and conducted emissions before formal EMC certification. The group makes regular use of a vector network analyser, near-field scanning bench, and FDTD and MoM solvers licensed through the faculty. She teaches courses in Electromagnetic Compatibility and High-Frequency Electronics at both undergraduate and master's level.

Radulović is interested in longer-term collaborative projects that involve real hardware from industrial partners rather than purely simulation-focused studies. Her scanning bench is available for external use on a cost-recovery basis when faculty teaching commitments permit. She is currently supervising two doctoral students expected to defend in 2026–2027.

LoRa devices operating in the 868 MHz European sub-GHz band are subject to harmonised standard EN 301 489-1 under the Radio Equipment Directive. This paper documents a structured compliance assessment of fifteen commercial and prototype LoRa end-node designs tested for radiated emissions, radiated immunity, and conducted disturbances. Testing was conducted in a semi-anechoic chamber accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025. Nine of fifteen devices exhibited radiated emissions exceeding the limit in the range 500–1000 MHz under worst-case payload and spreading factor combinations. A correlation between PCB layout quality metrics—specifically, return current path continuity and decoupling capacitor placement—and margin to the emission limit was observed. Immunity tests at 3 V/m field strength revealed functional degradation in four devices manifested as packet loss rates exceeding 10 %. The paper discusses how LoRa duty cycle restrictions interact with the quasi-peak detector integration time specified in the standard, a point of ambiguity that affects reproducibility across laboratories.

This paper investigates the degree to which near-field emission maps acquired with a planar probe array can predict far-field radiated emissions measured at a 3 m open-area test site (OATS). Forty-eight printed circuit board assemblies representing five product categories were characterised using a custom 64-element magnetic probe array with 5 mm probe pitch at heights of 3 mm and 8 mm above the board surface. Near-field data were processed with an equivalent dipole model to extrapolate far-field values. The mean absolute error between predicted and measured peak emissions was 4.2 dB, with 90 % of predictions falling within ±7 dB of OATS reference measurements in the 30–300 MHz range. Accuracy degraded above 500 MHz, where near-field spatial aliasing became significant at the chosen probe pitch. The method reduced test preparation time by approximately 60 % compared to full OATS campaigns in an iterative design cycle. Limitations related to enclosure shielding effects and cable routing variability are discussed.

Spread-spectrum clocking is applied in USB 3.2 controllers to reduce peak radiated emissions, but the resulting broadened spectral skirt can raise the noise floor experienced by collocated 2.4 GHz radio receivers. This paper quantifies the degradation in Wi-Fi receive sensitivity caused by USB 3.2 conducted and radiated interference in a laptop-class platform where the USB controller and Wi-Fi module share a common ground plane. Receiver sensitivity degradation was measured as a function of USB cable routing, ground plane slot geometry, and spread-spectrum modulation depth (0.5 %, 1.0 %, 2.0 %). At 0.5 % modulation depth, sensitivity degradation at the most affected Wi-Fi channel was 3.8 dB. Increasing modulation depth to 2.0 % reduced peak emission levels by 6.1 dB but increased the noise floor across the full 2.4–2.484 GHz band by 2.3 dB, resulting in a net degradation of 1.1 dB in worst-case channel sensitivity. Mitigation measures assessed include USB cable ferrite sleeve impedance, common-mode choke placement, and via stitching around the USB differential pair routing.

Semi-anechoic chambers of 3 m and 5 m class are widely used in Serbian and regional accredited testing laboratories, yet systematic multi-laboratory repeatability data for these facilities remain scarce. This study organised a proficiency test involving five laboratories in Serbia, Hungary, and Romania, each measuring radiated emissions from two identical reference radiators—a broadband comb generator and a stabilised 868 MHz transmitter—over the range 30 MHz to 1 GHz. Between-laboratory standard deviation ranged from 1.9 dB to 4.7 dB depending on frequency and polarisation, with the largest deviations observed below 80 MHz where chamber resonances are most significant. Within-laboratory repeatability standard deviation remained below 1.2 dB for all participants. The 5 m chambers showed a systematic 1.3 dB lower variability index than 3 m chambers across the full frequency range. The paper discusses causes of between-laboratory dispersion and proposes a standardised reference radiator procedure for routine verification of chamber performance between formal ISO 17025 audits.

Quantifying measurement uncertainty in radiated emissions tests is essential for reproducible compliance assessment under the Radio Equipment Directive. This study applies the CISPR 16-4-2 framework to a set of twelve 868 MHz short-range devices tested on a 3 m open-area test site and a semi-anechoic chamber. Six uncertainty contributors are evaluated: antenna factor calibration, receiver bandwidth, cable impedance mismatch, site imperfections expressed as normalised site attenuation deviation, ambient noise floor, and device positioning repeatability. The combined expanded uncertainty (k=2) ranged from 3.8 dB to 6.1 dB depending on frequency and device category. Comparison of results between the two test environments showed systematic differences of up to 2.3 dB for horizontally polarised emissions, consistent with ground-plane reflection variations. A simplified uncertainty budget worksheet suited to laboratory accreditation audits is presented. The findings suggest that the standard 6 dB margin applied in many pre-compliance workflows is insufficient for devices operating near the regulatory limit.

Ferrite beads are routinely used on power supply lines to suppress conducted emissions, but their impedance characteristics are nonlinear functions of DC bias current and signal amplitude, factors that are often neglected in circuit simulation models. This study characterises twelve surface-mount ferrite bead types from four manufacturers across the frequency range 1 MHz–1 GHz under DC bias from 0 to 3 A and signal amplitudes from −20 dBm to +10 dBm. Measurements were performed with a four-port VNA using a custom bias tee fixture. At 2 A DC bias, resistive impedance at 100 MHz was reduced by 55–80 % relative to the zero-bias datasheet value depending on bead type. A Jiles–Atherton based macro-model is fitted to the measurement data and validated in SPICE simulation against measured insertion loss of a representative power supply EMC filter. The model predicts insertion loss within 2 dB across the measured frequency range under all bias conditions tested. Implications for automotive 12 V rail filter design are discussed.

Practical implications for measurement matrix design are discussed.

Forty-eight zinc-oxide varistor discs rated 275 V rms, 6 kA (8/20 µs), were subjected to repetitive impulse stress to quantify degradation under conditions representative of indirect lightning exposure. Three stress protocols were used: 100 pulses at 1 kA, 50 pulses at 3 kA, and 20 pulses at 6 kA (all 8/20 µs). Varistor clamping voltage, leakage current at 0.9 times rated dc voltage, and thermal dissipation factor were measured before and after each protocol. Clamping voltage increased by 4–11% after 100 pulses at 1 kA and by 18–27% after 20 pulses at 6 kA. Leakage current increased by one order of magnitude in eight of sixteen specimens stressed at 6 kA, indicating incipient failure. Scanning electron microscopy of cross-sections revealed grain boundary degradation concentrated in a cylindrical core region. The results suggest that standard SPD replacement intervals based solely on visual inspection or power-frequency leakage tests are insufficient for sites with high indirect-lightning flash density above 2 flashes km⁻² yr⁻¹.

Two modelling strategies for predicting conducted emissions from LED retrofit lamp drivers are compared: a behavioural model based on measured Thevenin equivalent source impedance and voltage, and a circuit-level model derived from the reverse-engineered schematic of three driver types with rated power of 7 W, 12 W and 18 W. Both models are embedded in a low-voltage network simulation and evaluated against LISN measurements over 150 kHz to 30 MHz. The behavioural approach reproduces measured emission profiles with an average RMS error of 3.1 dB but requires individual characterisation of each unit. The circuit-level model achieves 4.7 dB average error without unit-specific measurement but is sensitive to uncertainty in parasitic component values. A hybrid procedure combining measured impedance data with a simplified circuit skeleton reduces average error to 2.6 dB. The study covers 15 driver samples from four unnamed market sources. Implications for aggregated emission prediction when large numbers of LED luminaires are installed on a single feeder are discussed, with a Monte Carlo analysis of 50 to 500 simultaneous loads.

Switch-mode power supplies (SMPS) are tested for conducted emissions according to CISPR 32 using three commercially available line impedance stabilisation networks (LISNs) of nominally identical 50 Ω/50 µH topology but from different manufacturers. Tests are performed on five SMPS samples with rated power between 30 W and 250 W. Measured quasi-peak levels at the same SMPS unit differ by up to 7.2 dB across LISNs in the 150 kHz to 500 kHz band, exceeding the 3 dB reproducibility figure often cited in the literature. The observed discrepancies are traced to differences in the LISN high-frequency impedance characteristic, particularly a self-resonance near 1.4 MHz in one unit. An additional test campaign varies the mains source impedance from 0.05 Ω to 0.8 Ω at 50 Hz by inserting series inductors, demonstrating that SMPS peak emission levels shift by up to 5 dB due to changes in rectifier operating point. These findings have implications for compliance margins and for the interpretation of borderline-pass test results.
Conducted emission test reproducibility for switch-mode power supplies: influence of LISN topology and mains impedance variation

Three-phase low-voltage feeders serving residential parking areas with electric vehicle charging infrastructure are studied using a combination of laboratory measurements and network simulation. On-board chargers of 3.3 kW, 7.4 kW and 11 kW rated power are characterised individually on a LISN test bench, and their emission spectra exported as Norton equivalent sources. A three-phase feeder model of 60 m length is parameterised from field impedance measurements and loaded with up to 12 simultaneous charger connections distributed across phases. Phase-to-phase coupling via the neutral conductor and earth return path is analysed and shown to introduce cross-phase disturbance voltages up to 8 dB below the directly driven phase in the 150 kHz to 500 kHz band. Feeder impedance variation due to the connection of reactive compensation capacitors shifts dominant emission peaks by up to 40 kHz. Compliance margins relative to EN 61000-3-11 group emission limits shrink by 6 dB when six or more chargers of the same type operate simultaneously. Results are discussed in the context of planned charging hub deployments.

Danijela Ninkov received her Dipl.Ing. and M.Sc. degrees in Electrical Engineering from the Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, in 1998 and 2003 respectively, and her Ph.D. from the same institution in 2008. She has held a Full Professor position since 2019 in the Department of Power, Electronics and Telecommunications. Her research group focuses on electromagnetic compatibility in low-voltage distribution networks, with particular attention to time-domain modelling of conducted disturbances, harmonic propagation, and the interaction between power electronic loads and grid regulation equipment. She teaches undergraduate and postgraduate courses in electromagnetic compatibility and power quality. The group operates a dedicated EMC measurement laboratory equipped with a line impedance stabilisation network, conducted emission analysers calibrated to CISPR standards, and a real-time power network emulator.
Conducted disturbance propagation from EV on-board chargers: network impedance dependency and phase-to-phase coupling

A time-domain simulation framework is developed to predict conducted emissions from single-phase uncontrolled rectifiers connected to a simplified residential low-voltage network. The network is represented by a ladder model with frequency-dependent line parameters derived from measurements on a 230 V, 50 Hz test feeder of approximately 120 m length. Rectifier loads ranging from 100 W to 2 kW are modelled as nonlinear voltage-dependent current sources parameterised from laboratory measurements. Simulated disturbance voltages at the mains terminal are compared against LISN-based measurements following CISPR 16-1-1 procedures over the 9 kHz to 30 MHz range. Agreement within 4 dB is achieved across the 150 kHz to 2 MHz sub-band, with larger deviations at higher frequencies attributed to parasitic capacitances not included in the ladder model. The study identifies the 450 kHz to 600 kHz interval as the most sensitive to load power level, with peak quasi-peak levels increasing by up to 11 dB when aggregate load increases from 500 W to 2 kW. The results suggest that existing CISPR limits may be approached under dense residential loading conditions.

Ripple control systems operating at 316.7 Hz and 750 Hz are widely used by distribution system operators in central Europe for remote load switching. This study investigates the extent to which supraharmonic emissions from switch-mode loads corrupt ripple control telegram reception in a 400 V test feeder modelled from parameters measured in a suburban distribution area near Novi Sad. A full time-domain model is built in MATLAB/Simulink incorporating a ripple control transmitter, feeder impedance, and four classes of switching loads: SMPS, LED drivers, PV micro-inverters, and EV on-board chargers. At 15% feeder loading with mixed loads, signal-to-interference ratio at the receiver input drops below the 20 dB design threshold assumed in EN 61000-5-1 for ripple control. Worst-case degradation of 28 dB is observed when multiple PV micro-inverters synchronise their switching near the ripple control frequency. Temporal correlation between load power cycles and interference bursts is demonstrated. The model is validated against a 4-hour measurement record from the test feeder with 4.5% mean absolute error in receiver input voltage.

This book chapter provides a systematic treatment of EMC problems specific to low-voltage distribution systems, intended for practising engineers and postgraduate students. The presentation proceeds from the physical mechanisms of conducted disturbance generation in power electronic equipment through to network propagation, coupling to sensitive loads, and measurement practice. The regulatory framework covering CISPR 11, CISPR 32, IEC 61000-3-2, IEC 61000-3-12 and EN 50160 is described with attention to applicability conditions and current revision status as of 2020. Frequency-domain and time-domain modelling approaches are compared for three representative scenarios: aggregated residential loading, industrial bus with variable-speed drives, and mixed-use low-voltage feeders with embedded generation. Common measurement pitfalls including grounding, LISN placement, and ambient noise subtraction are discussed with illustrative examples drawn from the authors' laboratory experience. The chapter concludes with an outline of open research questions including the standardisation of supraharmonic measurement methods and probabilistic compliance assessment.

Prefers projects with a clear measurement component rather than purely theoretical work. The EMC laboratory is shared with two other research groups and access scheduling should be discussed early in any collaboration. Available for new project commitments from early 2026 onward.

sources.value: Manual EMC design review is time-consuming and relies on reviewer expertise that varies across organisations. This paper describes a rule-based layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and a netlist, extracts geometric features related to emission risk, and outputs a numerical score and flagged violation list. Seventeen rules were derived from simulation studies and published guidelines, covering trace-to-plane spacing, clock trace routing distance from board edge, decoupling capacitor placement relative to device power pins, and via stub length. The tool was implemented in Python using open-source Gerber parsing libraries. Validation was performed by scoring 23 PCB designs of known emission performance; boards that failed CISPR 22 Class B measurements scored below the threshold in 19 out of 23 cases (83% sensitivity). False-positive rate was 22%. Run time for a 20-layer board with 4000 components averaged 38 seconds. The tool is intended as an early design gate rather than a replacement for simulation or pre-compliance measurement.

sources.value: This paper describes an integrated pre-compliance workflow for mixed-signal PCB development that combines three techniques used sequentially across the design cycle. In the early layout phase, an automated rule-checking tool flags geometric violations associated with known emission risks. At the prototype stage, near-field scanning at 3 mm standoff generates spatial emission maps that identify dominant radiating structures. Finally, FDTD simulation using geometry extracted from the identified hotspots provides frequency-resolved quantification and supports what-if analysis of corrective measures. The workflow was applied to four prototype boards developed in collaboration with two regional electronics companies. Across all four boards, the integrated workflow identified the dominant emission source correctly in each case; corrective measures applied on the basis of simulation results reduced the peak radiated emission at the pre-compliance test receiver by between 5.2 dB and 11.7 dB before formal OATS measurement. Time-to-compliance for the four designs averaged 2.1 fewer test-and-rework cycles compared to a historical baseline of designs developed without structured pre-compliance analysis. The workflow documentation and rule-checker code are deposited in an open repository.

sources.value: Power delivery network (PDN) impedance management in mixed-signal boards is examined through a combined measurement and simulation campaign. A test vehicle carrying an FPGA and two 12-bit ADC devices was designed with three decoupling capacitor placement strategies: bulk capacitors only, distributed 100 nF ceramic capacitors at 5 mm spacing, and a co-planar interdigitated capacitance structure formed by alternating power and ground copper pours. PDN impedance was measured from 100 kHz to 1 GHz using a one-port shunt method with a vector network analyser. Simultaneously, conducted noise on the 3.3 V rail was recorded with a 1 GHz oscilloscope probe during switching activity driven by a test pattern generator. The distributed ceramic strategy reduced peak PDN impedance from 840 mΩ to 210 mΩ at 480 MHz. Radiated emissions pre-compliance scans at 3 m confirmed a corresponding 4.8 dB reduction in broadband noise floor between 400 and 600 MHz. A compact circuit model of the PDN, fitted to measurement data, reproduces impedance to within 8% across the full bandwidth.

sources.value: This paper investigates whether automated near-field scan data acquired at 3 mm standoff can reliably predict far-field radiated emission rankings before a product undergoes formal OATS testing. Seven commercial-grade consumer electronics boards were scanned on a 150 mm × 150 mm grid with 2 mm step resolution at frequencies from 30 MHz to 1 GHz. Far-field transformation was applied using a planar near-to-far-field algorithm. Results were compared against 3 m OATS measurements performed at an accredited external laboratory. Rank-ordering agreement between pre-compliance near-field predictions and OATS results was 85% at the frequency of maximum emission for each board. Absolute amplitude agreement was within ±4.5 dB in 74% of cases, degrading to ±9 dB at frequencies above 700 MHz where enclosure resonances are significant. The findings suggest the methodology is reliable for early design triage but not as a substitute for final certification. Practical recommendations for scan grid density and probe calibration are provided.

Automotive DC–DC converters operating from a 48 V bus generate conducted emissions in the CISPR 25 frequency range (150 kHz–108 MHz) that must be suppressed before reaching the vehicle harness. This paper analyses five commercial common-mode choke families with inductances between 10 µH and 220 µH, characterising their impedance using two-port measurements and fitting a frequency-dependent equivalent circuit that captures core saturation effects at the DC bias levels typical of a 5 A converter. The fitted models were embedded in a SPICE simulation of a full input filter topology and validated against conducted emission measurements using a LISN. Key findings: chokes with ferrite cores exhibited a self-resonance artefact near 3 MHz that produced an emission peak rather than suppression; nanocrystalline core variants maintained greater than 40 dB insertion loss between 1 MHz and 30 MHz under full bias. A selection procedure based on impedance-at-bias rather than inductance-at-zero-bias is proposed and benchmarked against five converter test cases.

Moat-type splits in ground planes, often introduced to isolate analogue and digital regions, are known to increase radiated emissions when high-frequency signals cross them. This study quantifies the effect using method-of-moments modelling of a canonical two-layer board geometry with a 50 Ω microstrip carrying a 200 MHz square-wave clock. Moat widths of 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm, and 2.0 mm were evaluated with and without a 100 nF bridging capacitor placed at the crossing point. The MoM solver was validated by a controlled experiment in a GTEM cell. Without bridging, a 1 mm moat increased the peak radiated electric field at CISPR class B limits by 7.4 dB at the third harmonic (600 MHz). A single bridging capacitor reduced the excess to 1.8 dB. These results are mapped onto a simple analytical expression involving crossing current, moat length, and frequency, allowing designers to estimate the penalty before committing to layout. Limitations of the analytical approximation above 800 MHz are discussed.

LoRa devices operating in the 868 MHz European sub-GHz band are subject to harmonised standard EN 301 489-1 under the Radio Equipment Directive. This paper documents a structured compliance assessment of fifteen commercial and prototype LoRa end-node designs tested for radiated emissions, radiated immunity, and conducted disturbances. Testing was conducted in a semi-anechoic chamber accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025. Nine of fifteen devices exhibited radiated emissions exceeding the limit in the range 500–1000 MHz under worst-case payload and spreading factor combinations. A correlation between PCB layout quality metrics—specifically, return current path continuity and decoupling capacitor placement—and margin to the emission limit was observed. Immunity tests at 3 V/m field strength revealed functional degradation in four devices manifested as packet loss rates exceeding 10 %. The paper discusses how LoRa duty cycle restrictions interact with the quasi-peak detector integration time specified in the standard, a point of ambiguity that affects reproducibility across laboratories.

sources.value: This paper investigates the degree to which near-field emission maps acquired with a planar probe array can predict far-field radiated emissions measured at a 3 m open-area test site (OATS). Forty-eight printed circuit board assemblies representing five product categories were characterised using a custom 64-element magnetic probe array with 5 mm probe pitch at heights of 3 mm and 8 mm above the board surface. Near-field data were processed with an equivalent dipole model to extrapolate far-field values. The mean absolute error between predicted and measured peak emissions was 4.2 dB, with 90 % of predictions falling within ±7 dB of OATS reference measurements in the 30–300 MHz range. Accuracy degraded above 500 MHz, where near-field spatial aliasing became significant at the chosen probe pitch. The method reduced test preparation time by approximately 60 % compared to full OATS campaigns in an iterative design cycle. Limitations related to enclosure shielding effects and cable routing variability are discussed.

Spread-spectrum clocking is applied in USB 3.2 controllers to reduce peak radiated emissions, but the resulting broadened spectral skirt can raise the noise floor experienced by collocated 2.4 GHz radio receivers. This paper quantifies the degradation in Wi-Fi receive sensitivity caused by USB 3.2 conducted and radiated interference in a laptop-class platform where the USB controller and Wi-Fi module share a common ground plane. Receiver sensitivity degradation was measured as a function of USB cable routing, ground plane slot geometry, and spread-spectrum modulation depth (0.5 %, 1.0 %, 2.0 %). At 0.5 % modulation depth, sensitivity degradation at the most affected Wi-Fi channel was 3.8 dB. Increasing modulation depth to 2.0 % reduced peak emission levels by 6.1 dB but increased the noise floor across the full 2.4–2.484 GHz band by 2.3 dB, resulting in a net degradation of 1.1 dB in worst-case channel sensitivity. Mitigation measures assessed include USB cable ferrite sleeve impedance, common-mode choke placement, and via stitching around the USB differential pair routing.

sources.value: Semi-anechoic chambers of 3 m and 5 m class are widely used in Serbian and regional accredited testing laboratories, yet systematic multi-laboratory repeatability data for these facilities remain scarce. This study organised a proficiency test involving five laboratories in Serbia, Hungary, and Romania, each measuring radiated emissions from two identical reference radiators—a broadband comb generator and a stabilised 868 MHz transmitter—over the range 30 MHz to 1 GHz. Between-laboratory standard deviation ranged from 1.9 dB to 4.7 dB depending on frequency and polarisation, with the largest deviations observed below 80 MHz where chamber resonances are most significant. Within-laboratory repeatability standard deviation remained below 1.2 dB for all participants. The 5 m chambers showed a systematic 1.3 dB lower variability index than 3 m chambers across the full frequency range. The paper discusses causes of between-laboratory dispersion and proposes a standardised reference radiator procedure for routine verification of chamber performance between formal ISO 17025 audits.

sources.value: Quantifying measurement uncertainty in radiated emissions tests is essential for reproducible compliance assessment under the Radio Equipment Directive. This study applies the CISPR 16-4-2 framework to a set of twelve 868 MHz short-range devices tested on a 3 m open-area test site and a semi-anechoic chamber. Six uncertainty contributors are evaluated: antenna factor calibration, receiver bandwidth, cable impedance mismatch, site imperfections expressed as normalised site attenuation deviation, ambient noise floor, and device positioning repeatability. The combined expanded uncertainty (k=2) ranged from 3.8 dB to 6.1 dB depending on frequency and device category. Comparison of results between the two test environments showed systematic differences of up to 2.3 dB for horizontally polarised emissions, consistent with ground-plane reflection variations. A simplified uncertainty budget worksheet suited to laboratory accreditation audits is presented. The findings suggest that the standard 6 dB margin applied in many pre-compliance workflows is insufficient for devices operating near the regulatory limit.

sources.value: Ferrite beads are routinely used on power supply lines to suppress conducted emissions, but their impedance characteristics are nonlinear functions of DC bias current and signal amplitude, factors that are often neglected in circuit simulation models. This study characterises twelve surface-mount ferrite bead types from four manufacturers across the frequency range 1 MHz–1 GHz under DC bias from 0 to 3 A and signal amplitudes from −20 dBm to +10 dBm. Measurements were performed with a four-port VNA using a custom bias tee fixture. At 2 A DC bias, resistive impedance at 100 MHz was reduced by 55–80 % relative to the zero-bias datasheet value depending on bead type. A Jiles–Atherton based macro-model is fitted to the measurement data and validated in SPICE simulation against measured insertion loss of a representative power supply EMC filter. The model predicts insertion loss within 2 dB across the measured frequency range under all bias conditions tested. Implications for automotive 12 V rail filter design are discussed.

The relationship between the current control loop bandwidth of grid-following single-phase inverters and their conducted emission characteristics in the 150 kHz to 2 MHz range is examined through a parametric simulation study validated by laboratory measurements. A full-cycle time-domain inverter model is implemented in PLECS and exercised across current controller bandwidths from 500 Hz to 8 kHz, LCL filter corner frequencies from 4 kHz to 20 kHz, and DC bus voltages of 200 V, 350 V and 600 V. Conducted emission spectra at the AC terminals are extracted via an embedded LISN model and compared with CISPR 11 Class B limits. Increasing controller bandwidth from 1 kHz to 5 kHz reduces low-frequency distortion but increases emissions in the 200 kHz to 600 kHz band by 3 to 11 dB depending on LCL corner frequency. A low-pass post-filter of 47 µH/10 nF placed after the LCL filter reduces peak emission levels by 8 dB with less than 0.3% increase in fundamental voltage drop. Laboratory validation on a 2 kW prototype confirms simulation trends with deviations below 4 dB across 90% of the measured frequency range.

sources.value: Running a full FEM simulation for each combination of insulator geometry and pollution condition is computationally expensive for grid-scale insulator fleet assessments. This paper investigates whether a gradient-boosted regression model trained on an FEM-generated dataset can accurately predict peak tangential electric field values. The training dataset comprised 2 400 2D FEM simulations varying six parameters: shed diameter ratio, pitch, shed count, pollution conductivity, film thickness, and power frequency voltage. An 80/20 train–test split was used; hyperparameters were tuned by fivefold cross-validation. The trained model predicted peak field values with a mean absolute error of 0.031 kV/mm and R² = 0.97 on the held-out test set, with inference times under 2 ms. The approach was validated against an independent set of 60 FEM cases not used in training, confirming generalisability within the parameter ranges studied. Limitations at extrapolation boundaries are discussed.

sources.value: Leakage current waveform distortion under pollution is widely used as a diagnostic indicator, but its relationship to computed electric field distribution is not well established. This study correlates results from a validated 2D FEM model with simultaneous leakage current measurements on six 20 kV composite insulator samples subjected to controlled saline fog pollution in a climate chamber. Pollution layers with ESDD values of 0.025, 0.05, and 0.1 mg/cm² were tested at 50 Hz. Third-harmonic leakage current content increased from 3% to 18% as ESDD rose, while simulated peak tangential fields grew from 0.6 to 1.4 kV/mm at the shed edges. A linear regression between third-harmonic amplitude and simulated field peak yielded R² = 0.91, suggesting that field computation could support interpretation of online leakage current monitoring data.

sources.value: A three-branch RC ladder model extended with fractional-order capacitors is proposed to account simultaneously for fast charge storage, slow pore diffusion, and long-term leakage in electrochemical double-layer capacitors. Model parameters were determined from impedance spectra and from constant-current charge–discharge experiments performed on eight cells (1 F to 50 F) over 200 cycle sequences. The fractional exponents in the first and second branches differed by up to 0.12, indicating distinct pore populations. Voltage redistribution curves measured after current interruption were reproduced by the model with a root-mean-square error below 3 mV across all cells. The leakage conductance extracted from very low frequency measurements (down to 0.5 mHz) agreed with 72-hour self-discharge data to within 15%. The model is intended for use in energy management algorithms that must account for charge redistribution losses.

sources.value: This chapter reviews and extends Bayesian formulations of compressed sensing as applied to multiband spectrum recovery in cognitive radio. A hierarchical Bayesian model is constructed in which each frequency bin's power level is assigned a Laplace prior, enforcing sparsity without requiring explicit knowledge of the sparsity level. Posterior inference is performed via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling using a Gibbs sampler with 5000 burn-in and 10000 retained samples. The approach is compared against LASSO, OMP, and iterative reweighted least squares (IRLS) on synthetic multiband signals with 1 to 8 simultaneously active bands, each 5 MHz wide, within a 200 MHz observation window. The Bayesian method outperforms LASSO by 2.1 dB in NMSE at SNR = 5 dB and provides calibrated posterior uncertainty intervals, which are relevant for secondary user access decisions. Computational cost remains the primary limitation for real-time deployment; strategies for approximate inference are outlined.

Boards intended for environments with frequent thermal excursions require design-for-testability decisions that balance initial test coverage with the need to maintain that coverage throughout the product lifetime as solder joints and contact pads degrade. This preprint consolidates data from five years of thermal cycling experiments and production test monitoring at two electronics manufacturing partners to derive a set of quantitative DFT guidelines. For each of twelve layout and routing decisions—including test pad size, via-in-pad avoidance, and scan chain segmentation—the study reports the effect on initial boundary-scan coverage, estimated coverage at 1,000 thermal cycles, and the probability of a probe contact failure per 100,000 test operations. The guidelines are expressed as scoring criteria compatible with standard DFT review checklists. Validation on three new board designs showed that following the guidelines improved predicted 1,000-cycle coverage by an average of 9.4 percentage points relative to designs reviewed without the guidelines.

sources.value: The project addresses the degradation of in-circuit and boundary-scan test coverage that occurs as solder joints, contact pads, and board laminates age under repeated thermal excursions. The core deliverables are a set of empirically validated coverage-lifetime models parameterised by thermal profile severity, board material, and component package type, and a software tool that uses these models to predict coverage at any point in a product's operating lifetime. The tool was demonstrated on board designs provided by two industrial partners. The project also produced a revised DFT guideline document tailored to boards used in outdoor electronics enclosures in continental European climate conditions.

Functional test sequences for mixed-signal boards are often designed by hand, resulting in redundant measurements and long test times. This paper formulates functional test sequencing as an integer linear programming problem in which the objective is to minimise total test execution time subject to constraints on fault coverage, power sequencing dependencies, and signal settling times. The ILP model was solved with a branch-and-bound solver for six industrial board designs ranging from 18 to 64 functional test steps. Optimised sequences reduced mean test time by 27 % compared to original hand-crafted sequences while maintaining or improving fault coverage in five of the six cases. The largest board saw test time cut from 142 to 98 seconds. Constraint violation penalties were calibrated against data from 1,200 production test records to ensure that power sequencing margins were never violated. The method is board-agnostic and requires only a netlist and a test-step dependency graph as inputs.

sources.value: IEEE 1149.4 extends boundary-scan to analogue pins, but its adoption in volume production has been limited by uncertainty about achievable fault coverage on practical board topologies. This study analyses test coverage attainable under the 1149.4 standard for five analogue subcircuit categories: RC filters, op-amp stages, ADC input conditioning networks, power management feedback loops, and sensor signal conditioning chains. Each category was represented by ten reference circuits implemented on test vehicles. Coverage was measured by fault injection: 1,240 resistor opens/shorts and 880 capacitor deviations spanning ±20 % to ±80 % of nominal value. Achieved coverage ranged from 73 % for power-management loops to 94 % for RC filter networks, with the main limitation being the bandwidth of the analogue test bus relative to circuit operating frequency. A set of design-for-test recommendations is derived from the results, targeting layouts that improve 1149.4 coverage by an average of 11 percentage points.

sources.value: This paper compares five supervised classification algorithms—logistic regression, random forest, gradient-boosted trees, a shallow multilayer perceptron, and a support vector machine with RBF kernel—for classifying PCB assembly defects from flying-probe in-circuit test measurement vectors. The dataset comprised 11,340 test records from 18 months of production, annotated with nine defect categories confirmed by automated optical inspection and manual rework records. Feature sets included 28 electrical measurements per record: impedance magnitude, phase, DC resistance, and transient current slope at multiple test points. Random forest and gradient-boosted trees achieved the highest macro-averaged F1 scores of 0.913 and 0.908 respectively on a stratified held-out test set. The MLP performed comparably at 0.901 but required substantially longer training time. A practical deployment scheme is described in which the classifier runs as a post-processing module on the tester host PC, adding less than 200 ms per board. Class imbalance handling via SMOTE is evaluated, showing consistent benefit for rare defect categories.

sources.value: This paper presents a quantitative framework for evaluating boundary-scan controllability and observability on mixed-signal printed circuit board assemblies where analogue subcircuits interrupt digital scan chains. The method assigns a weighted coverage score to each net segment based on the ratio of scan-accessible driver–receiver pairs to the total number of electrical nodes. Experiments were conducted on three reference boards populated with 128, 256, and 512 component pins respectively, using a commercial JTAG controller operating at 10 MHz TCK. Coverage scores were compared against hand-calculated fault-injection results for twelve common defect classes including opens, shorts, and stuck-at faults. The framework identified a 14–22 % gap between nominal boundary-scan coverage estimates and empirically verified detection rates on nets that cross analogue power domains. A correction factor derived from net impedance profiles is proposed and validated on an automotive-grade sensor interface board. The approach requires no modifications to existing IEEE 1149.1 infrastructure.

sources.value: Solder joint degradation under repeated thermal excursions alters joint resistance in ways that can shift in-circuit test measurements outside tolerance windows, producing false failures or masking real defects. This study subjected 120 FR-4 boards, each carrying 84 SOIC-16 and 48 QFN-32 packages, to 0–100 °C thermal cycling at 2 cycles per hour for 500, 1000, and 1500 cycles. Joint resistance was measured with a four-wire Kelvin technique after each milestone. In-circuit test pass rates were re-evaluated at each stage using a bed-of-nails fixture on a commercial ICT platform. Results show that mean joint resistance increased by 38 mΩ after 1500 cycles for QFN pads, causing a 6.1 % increase in false-open calls. A temperature-corrected threshold model is presented that reduces false calls to below 1 % across all cycle counts tested. The model parameters are extracted from a 15-minute characterisation run on a fresh board.

sources.value: High-density board-to-board connectors with pitches below 0.5 mm are difficult to access with flying-probe or bed-of-nails fixtures, making boundary-scan the only practical interconnect verification method. This work describes an algorithm that automatically generates optimised JTAG test vectors for connector nets by traversing the board netlist graph and selecting driver–receiver pairs that maximise fault coverage while minimising vector length. The algorithm was implemented in Python 3.8 and validated on four industrial backplane designs containing between 800 and 2400 connector pins. Generated vector sets achieved 97.3 % stuck-at coverage on average, compared to 89.1 % for vendor-supplied default vectors, while reducing vector count by 31 %. The equivalent series inductance (ESL) of the DC-link capacitor bank in a pulse-width-modulated inverter drive is often overlooked in EMC pre-compliance analysis yet contributes measurably to conducted emissions above 5 MHz. This study quantifies the effect by replacing a standard electrolytic capacitor bank (ESL ≈ 45 nH) with a film capacitor arrangement (ESL ≈ 8 nH) in a 4 kW test drive and recording the full conducted emission spectrum from 150 kHz to 30 MHz under identical load conditions. Peak differential-mode emissions between 10 MHz and 30 MHz were reduced by 6–11 dB with the lower-ESL bank. Impedance spectroscopy measurements confirmed the resonance shift from 9.2 MHz to above 30 MHz. A circuit-level simulation model incorporating measured parasitic parameters reproduced the spectral features within ±2 dB. The findings are directly applicable to PCB layout guidelines for compact drive modules targeting IEC 61800-3 Category C2 limits.

sources.value: The project addressed the gap between laboratory IEC 61800-3 compliance and field performance of EMC filters for SiC MOSFET motor drives. The work covered three main activities: systematic conducted emission characterisation of SiC drives from 2.2 kW to 22 kW, development of a measurement uncertainty budget specific to high-di/dt inverter systems, and design and experimental validation of filter topologies robust to realistic PE impedance variation encountered in Serbian industrial installations. Deliverables included a filter design procedure, a dataset of emission spectra and PE impedance profiles made publicly available, and two validated simulation models. The project supported two PhD students and produced eight peer-reviewed publications.

This paper presents a structured procedure for dimensioning passive EMC input filters for variable-speed drives to meet IEC 61800-3 Category C2 quasi-peak limits. The procedure uses measured CM and DM source impedances and a target attenuation profile derived from the gap between unfiltered emission spectra and the regulatory limit line, with a 6 dB safety margin applied throughout. Filter topologies (LC, LCL, and CL stages) are compared for a 15 kW test drive, and component values are selected to avoid resonances within the 150 kHz–2 MHz band that could cause limit exceedances at intermediate frequencies. Prototype filters were wound on nanocrystalline toroidal cores and verified by insertion-loss measurement per IEC 60939-3 before integration. Final compliance measurements confirmed that all quasi-peak and average readings were at least 5 dB below the Category C2 limit across the full 150 kHz–30 MHz range. Total filter volume was 0.38 litres and mass 0.61 kg for the 15 kW case.

Long motor cables are common in industrial installations and amplify common-mode conducted disturbances by adding distributed capacitance to ground. This experimental study quantifies the effect for shielded and unshielded cables of lengths 5 m, 20 m, and 50 m connected to a 5.5 kW drive. CM conducted emission levels at the drive input were measured for each combination. Unshielded 50 m cables increased broadband CM noise by 10–14 dB relative to the 5 m reference below 1 MHz, primarily due to cable-to-ground capacitance estimated at 3.4 nF for the 50 m case. Shield grounding at both ends reduced CM emissions by 5–9 dB across 150 kHz–5 MHz for the 20 m cable. A transmission-line model incorporating per-unit-length parameters measured by time-domain reflectometry reproduced the resonant structure of the emission spectrum within ±3 dB. Practical wiring recommendations derived from the data are summarised for installation engineers.

sources.value: The attenuation provided by Y-capacitors in common-mode EMC filters depends on the impedance of the protective earth (PE) connection, which varies substantially between industrial installations. This paper characterises PE impedance at 47 industrial sites across northern Serbia using a vector network analyser, finding that impedance magnitude at 1 MHz ranges from 0.4 Ω to 18 Ω and exhibits significant inductive character above 500 kHz. A modified filter topology using a split CM choke with partial differential-mode rejection reduces this variability to within ±2 dB.

A 400 V / 48 V, 500 W DC–DC converter using 650 V GaN HEMTs and switching at 1 MHz is characterised for conducted and radiated electromagnetic emissions per CISPR 32 Class B limits. Conducted emissions were measured using a line-impedance stabilisation network in the 150 kHz–30 MHz band. Differential-mode and common-mode noise contributions were separated using a current probe and a 180° hybrid coupler. Radiated emissions were measured in a semi-anechoic chamber in the 30 MHz–1 GHz band. Without input filtering, differential-mode conducted noise at 1 MHz exceeded the Class B quasi-peak limit by 18 dBµV. A two-stage LC input filter reduced differential-mode noise by 24 dB and common-mode noise by 19 dB, achieving compliance with 4 dB margin. Parasitic capacitance of the heat-sink was identified as the dominant common-mode noise path and a Y-capacitor between heat-sink and DC bus reduced common-mode noise by a further 7 dB. Correlation between near-field scan results and far-field measurements is discussed.

sources.value: Common-source inductance (CSI) introduced by PCB interconnects degrades switching-speed and increases switching energy in GaN half-bridge circuits. This paper presents a parametric finite-element study of CSI as a function of five geometric variables: via diameter, via pitch, power-loop width, source-sense routing length, and copper pour layer count. Seventeen PCB variants were fabricated and CSI was measured by the impedance-analyser short-circuit method at 1 MHz. CSI ranged from 0.4 nH for a four-layer optimised layout to 3.1 nH for a two-layer reference layout. An isolated gate-driver power supply achieving reinforced insulation per IEC 60950-1 is described for use with 650 V enhancement-mode GaN half-bridge modules. The design uses a 4 MHz resonant Royer oscillator driving a coreless PCB transformer with a creepage distance of 8 mm and a measured partial-discharge inception voltage of 4.2 kV. sources.value: This paper presents a systematic measurement campaign of switching energies in a 600 V enhancement-mode GaN HEMT half-bridge using a double-pulse test fixture. Turn-on losses Eon and turn-off losses Eoff were measured across a gate-resistance range of 0–22 Ω, a drain current range of 2–25 A, and junction temperatures of 25 °C and 100 °C. At 15 A and 400 V with a 4.7 Ω gate resistance, Eon was 4.8 µJ and Eoff was 1.9 µJ, giving a total switching loss of 6.7 µJ per event. Parasitic common-source inductance of the PCB layout was extracted via network-analyser S-parameter measurements and ranged from 0.8 to 2.3 nH across three board variants. A piece-wise linear switching model was fitted to the experimental data with relative error below 6 % over the full test matrix. The calorimetric cross-validation agreed with the electrical integration method within 4 %. Results are compared with datasheet figures and discrepancies exceeding 20 % at high current are highlighted.

The influence of dielectric thickness, copper weight, and layer ordering on radiated emissions from a standardised eight-layer stack-up is evaluated using a parametric FDTD study. A benchmark circuit, consisting of a 500 MHz single-ended clock distribution tree with three fanout nodes, was instantiated on 24 stack-up variants spanning dielectric thicknesses from 0.1 mm to 0.3 mm and copper weights of 0.5 oz and 1 oz. Each variant was simulated to obtain the radiated electric field at 3 m. Stack-ups with the signal layers closest to ground reference planes showed the lowest far-field peak, with a maximum suppression of 8.9 dB relative to the worst-performing arrangement. Dielectric thickness had a stronger influence than copper weight; halving the spacing between a signal layer and its reference plane reduced emissions by an average of 5.2 dB at the fifth harmonic. Simulation time per variant averaged 4.2 hours on a 16-core workstation. The results confirm that stack-up selection is an effective early-stage emission control tool that costs nothing in component budget.

This book chapter reviews the surge protection requirements applicable to low-voltage photovoltaic systems in Serbia, Romania, Hungary, and North Macedonia, comparing provisions of IEC 61643-32:2017 (SPD selection and application at PV power systems), IEC 62305 (lightning protection), and the national grid connection codes of the four countries as in force in 2024. Differences are identified in three areas: the method for determining the required impulse current class of DC-side SPDs, the treatment of floating versus grounded DC systems, and the earthing resistance thresholds triggering mandatory installation of additional earth electrodes. The chapter includes a worked example for a 100 kWp ground-mounted plant at a site with a flash density of 1.8 km⁻² yr⁻¹, showing that the four national frameworks produce SPD selection outcomes ranging from type 1 to type 2 for the same installation. Tables cross-referencing standard clauses to practical design decisions are provided for practising engineers.

sources.value: Reliable compressed sensing reconstruction in cognitive radio depends on accurate prior knowledge of spectrum sparsity. This work reports a 14-day passive measurement campaign conducted in Novi Sad using a calibrated wideband receiver covering 80–860 MHz at a resolution bandwidth of 100 kHz. Occupancy was defined by an energy detection threshold set 6 dB above the measured noise floor. Across the observation window, mean occupancy was 11.3%, with pronounced temporal clustering around broadcast television slots and GSM uplink intervals. Frequency-domain sparsity followed a Zipf-like distribution with exponent 0.81. Diurnal occupancy variance exceeded 40% in the FM radio sub-band but was below 8% for digital television multiplexes. The data set provides empirical support for sparse prior assumptions used in sub-Nyquist sensing architectures and is made available in anonymised form as a supplementary dataset. Practical implications for measurement matrix design are discussed.

sources.value: Forty-eight zinc-oxide varistor discs rated 275 V rms, 6 kA (8/20 µs), were subjected to repetitive impulse stress to quantify degradation under conditions representative of indirect lightning exposure. Three stress protocols were used: 100 pulses at 1 kA, 50 pulses at 3 kA, and 20 pulses at 6 kA (all 8/20 µs). Varistor clamping voltage, leakage current at 0.9 times rated dc voltage, and thermal dissipation factor were measured before and after each protocol. Clamping voltage increased by 4–11% after 100 pulses at 1 kA and by 18–27% after 20 pulses at 6 kA. Leakage current increased by one order of magnitude in eight of sixteen specimens stressed at 6 kA, indicating incipient failure. Scanning electron microscopy of cross-sections revealed grain boundary degradation concentrated in a cylindrical core region. The results suggest that standard SPD replacement intervals based solely on visual inspection or power-frequency leakage tests are insufficient for sites with high indirect-lightning flash density above 2 flashes km⁻² yr⁻¹.

Two modelling strategies for predicting conducted emissions from LED retrofit lamp drivers are compared: a behavioural model based on measured Thevenin equivalent source impedance and voltage, and a circuit-level model derived from the reverse-engineered schematic of three driver types with rated power of 7 W, 12 W and 18 W. Both models are embedded in a low-voltage network simulation and evaluated against LISN measurements over 150 kHz to 30 MHz. The behavioural approach reproduces measured emission profiles with an average RMS error of 3.1 dB but requires individual characterisation of each unit. The circuit-level model achieves 4.7 dB average error without unit-specific measurement but is sensitive to uncertainty in parasitic component values. A hybrid procedure combining measured impedance data with a simplified circuit skeleton reduces average error to 2.6 dB. The study covers 15 driver samples from four unnamed market sources. Implications for aggregated emission prediction when large numbers of LED luminaires are installed on a single feeder are discussed, with a Monte Carlo analysis of 50 to 500 simultaneous loads.

sources.value: Switch-mode power supplies (SMPS) are tested for conducted emissions according to CISPR 32 using three commercially available line impedance stabilisation networks (LISNs) of nominally identical 50 Ω/50 µH topology but from different manufacturers. Tests are performed on five SMPS samples with rated power between 30 W and 250 W. Measured quasi-peak levels at the same SMPS unit differ by up to 7.2 dB across LISNs in the 150 kHz to 500 kHz band, exceeding the 3 dB reproducibility figure often cited in the literature. The observed discrepancies are traced to differences in the LISN high-frequency impedance characteristic, particularly a self-resonance near 1.4 MHz in one unit. An additional test campaign varies the mains source impedance from 0.05 Ω to 0.8 Ω at 50 Hz by inserting series inductors, demonstrating that SMPS peak emission levels shift by up to 5 dB due to changes in rectifier operating point. These findings have implications for compliance margins and for the interpretation of borderline-pass test results.

Three-phase low-voltage feeders serving residential parking areas with electric vehicle charging infrastructure are studied using a combination of laboratory measurements and network simulation. On-board chargers of 3.3 kW, 7.4 kW and 11 kW rated power are characterised individually on a LISN test bench, and their emission spectra exported as Norton equivalent sources. A three-phase feeder model of 60 m length is parameterised from field impedance measurements and loaded with up to 12 simultaneous charger connections distributed across phases. Phase-to-phase coupling via the neutral conductor and earth return path is analysed and shown to introduce cross-phase disturbance voltages up to 8 dB below the directly driven phase in the 150 kHz to 500 kHz band. Feeder impedance variation due to the connection of reactive compensation capacitors shifts dominant emission peaks by up to 40 kHz. Compliance margins relative to EN 61000-3-11 group emission limits shrink by 6 dB when six or more chargers of the same type operate simultaneously. Results are discussed in the context of planned charging hub deployments.

A time-domain simulation framework is developed to predict conducted emissions from single-phase uncontrolled rectifiers connected to a simplified residential low-voltage network. The network is represented by a ladder model with frequency-dependent line parameters derived from measurements on a 230 V, 50 Hz test feeder of approximately 120 m length. Rectifier loads ranging from 100 W to 2 kW are modelled as nonlinear voltage-dependent current sources parameterised from laboratory measurements. Simulated disturbance voltages at the mains terminal are compared against LISN-based measurements following CISPR 16-1-1 procedures over the 9 kHz to 30 MHz range. Agreement within 4 dB is achieved across the 150 kHz to 2 MHz sub-band, with larger deviations at higher frequencies attributed to parasitic capacitances not included in the ladder model. The study identifies the 450 kHz to 600 kHz interval as the most sensitive to load power level, with peak quasi-peak levels increasing by up to 11 dB when aggregate load increases from 500 W to 2 kW. The results suggest that existing CISPR limits may be approached under dense residential loading conditions.

sources.value: Ripple control systems operating at 316.7 Hz and 750 Hz are widely used by distribution system operators in central Europe for remote load switching. This study investigates the extent to which supraharmonic emissions from switch-mode loads corrupt ripple control telegram reception in a 400 V test feeder modelled from parameters measured in a suburban distribution area near Novi Sad. A full time-domain model is built in MATLAB/Simulink incorporating a ripple control transmitter, feeder impedance, and four classes of switching loads: SMPS, LED drivers, PV micro-inverters, and EV on-board chargers. At 15% feeder loading with mixed loads, signal-to-interference ratio at the receiver input drops below the 20 dB design threshold assumed in EN 61000-5-1 for ripple control. Worst-case degradation of 28 dB is observed when multiple PV micro-inverters synchronise their switching near the ripple control frequency. Temporal correlation between load power cycles and interference bursts is demonstrated. The model is validated against a 4-hour measurement record from the test feeder with 4.5% mean absolute error in receiver input voltage.

sources.value: This book chapter provides a systematic treatment of EMC problems specific to low-voltage distribution systems, intended for practising engineers and postgraduate students. The presentation proceeds from the physical mechanisms of conducted disturbance generation in power electronic equipment through to network propagation, coupling to sensitive loads, and measurement practice. The regulatory framework covering CISPR 11, CISPR 32, IEC 61000-3-2, IEC 61000-3-12 and EN 50160 is described with attention to applicability conditions and current revision status as of 2020. Frequency-domain and time-domain modelling approaches are compared for three representative scenarios: aggregated residential loading, industrial bus with variable-speed drives, and mixed-use low-voltage feeders with embedded generation. Common measurement pitfalls including grounding, LISN placement, and ambient noise subtraction are discussed with illustrative examples drawn from the authors' laboratory experience. The chapter concludes with an outline of open research questions including the standardisation of supraharmonic measurement methods and probabilistic compliance assessment.
